steps.title: Reading comprehension — the working method
steps.intro: 6–7 minutes per passage, reading included: read only what the questions need.

tables.title: Question types
head: Type
How to spot it
What to read
rows: From one sentence before; several lines → just those
No place given, no "according to the passage"
Between the question before and after
"according to the passage" (the last question may omit it)
Skip, mark, solve last — use what you gathered

tables.title: Steps
head: Do this
rows: Read the question — without the choices
Read the part of the passage it points to
Read the question with the choices, and answer
Repeat for every specific question, in order

tips: Answer only from the passage, never from general knowledge.
Questions follow the passage order — general questions can appear anywhere.
A name you never met in the passage is probably invented for the question — don't hunt for it.
Short on time: read the first sentence of each paragraph (or first + last).

steps.stem: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the sentence "The pattern, however, is a tendency rather than a law … the pattern predicts" (paragraph 1)?
choices: Not every island species conforms to the pattern: many have not changed in size at all, and some have even changed in the opposite direction
Most island species conform to the pattern, and those that do not conform to it have changed in size in the opposite direction
Since many island species have not changed in size, the direction of change that the pattern predicts is often the wrong one
A few island species have changed in size in the predicted direction, but a great many have not changed in size at all
explanation: The sentence names two exceptions: many species that did not change and a few that changed the other way. (2) adds "most" and merges the two groups, (3) turns "no change" into evidence of the wrong direction, and (4) attaches "a few" to the species that follow the pattern.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 2, why do large animals tend to become smaller on islands?
choices: Because the area of an island is too small to hold animals of a large size
Because on an island, smaller animals find it easier to hide from predators
Because when food runs short and there is nowhere else to go, the individuals that need less food are more likely to survive and reproduce
Because the food available on islands is of poorer quality than the food available on the mainland
explanation: The paragraph links size to the amount of food: a smaller body gets through a lean season, and over generations the population shrinks. (1) is what the ration hypothesis denies, (2) belongs to the other explanation (paragraph 3), and (4) speaks of quality, which the paragraph never mentions.

steps.stem: Two populations of the same species of wild goat live on the islands of Arvo and Deska, which are equal in area. The goats on Arvo are considerably smaller than the goats on Deska. According to the "ration hypothesis," which of the following could explain this?
choices: Arvo is farther from the mainland than Deska is
Arvo provides less food for each goat than Deska does
There are more predators on Arvo than on Deska
Deska consists mostly of bare rock, whereas Arvo is covered with dense vegetation
explanation: Under the ration hypothesis, the food available to each animal, not the island's area, decides how strongly small bodies are favored. (4) reverses the two islands, and (1) and (3) name factors the hypothesis does not use; more predators would, if anything, favor larger bodies.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 3, which of the following is not correct regarding the explanation from predators?
choices: It holds that the absence of predators can account both for the growth of small animals and for the shrinking of large ones
It assumes that a very large body can protect a grazing animal from predators
It predicts that species living on islands without predators will change in size
It is more convincing for the shrinking of large animals than for the growth of small ones
explanation: The paragraph says this of the explanation from food, and presents the predator explanation's merit as covering both directions. (1), (2) and (3) are each stated in the paragraph.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 4, which of the following findings would have supported the explanation from predators?
choices: Lizards on the snake-free islands differ in size from lizards on islands with snakes that have a similar supply of insects
The size of the lizards on each island corresponds to the number of insects on that island
The snakes reached the islands only a relatively short time ago
The lizards are of the same size on all of the islands in the chain
explanation: The researchers said the predator explanation required a size difference between snake-free and snake islands even where food was similar. (2) is the actual finding, which supports the food explanation; (3) is the researchers' caution, which may excuse the predator explanation but does not support it; (4) supports neither explanation.

steps.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Animals on islands always change in size, in whichever direction the local supply of food dictates
The size of an animal is not a fixed feature of its species but a compromise among pressures, which the conditions on an island can alter
The explanation from food has been shown to be correct, and the explanation from predators has been refuted
Island animals are smaller than their mainland relatives because islands offer less food and fewer predators
explanation: The last paragraph draws the general lesson that the whole passage builds toward. (1) says "always," which paragraph 1 denies; (3) overstates a study whose conclusion is limited to "these islands, at least"; (4) ignores the small animals that grow larger.

steps.stem: What is the answer implied by the passage to the question "Can one say at which telling … but not the fourth?" (paragraph 2)?
choices: Yes - it is the first telling, since only the first telling is based on the original trace
Yes - it is the telling in which a detail was added to the story for the first time, rather than dropped from it
No - because a story that is told many times does not change from one telling to the next
No - because the story changes by steps too small to notice, so there is no telling at which it becomes a different story
explanation: The critics answer the question themselves: no such point can be found, because the changes accumulate by tiny steps. (3) gives the right "no" for the storage view's reason, which the critics reject; (1) and (2) invent a boundary the passage denies.

steps.stem: Yael defends the storage view. To illustrate her position, she says that she can tell with certainty whether she remembers the code of her building's front door, since she need only enter it and see whether the door opens. Which of the following claims points to the difficulty in Yael's argument?
choices: The door might open for a reason that has nothing to do with the code Yael entered
A short code leaves fragments so complete that it hardly needs rebuilding, so success in recalling it does not show how memory for events works
A code that has been entered many times is remembered more accurately than a code that has been entered only once
According to the critics, a person may remember a code with complete confidence and nevertheless remember it wrongly
explanation: Like the memorized list, a door code is a case that Meron's account also accommodates, so it cannot decide between the views or show that memory for events works by retrieval. (4) sounds like the critics, but the door test would expose such an error, so it is no difficulty for Yael; (1) and (3) are beside the point.

steps.stem: What does the sentence "A witness who describes shattered glass … a record that was never made" (paragraph 2) illustrate?
choices: That an error of memory may consist of something added to what occurred, and not only of something missing from it
That a memory changes slightly each time the event is told again
That witnesses to real accidents are less reliable than participants in laboratory experiments
That forgetting is a failure to find a record that was stored in the mind
explanation: The sentence sums up the second objection: errors are not only omissions, since people remember things that never happened. (2) is the first objection, (4) is the storage view itself, and (3) compares two groups the passage never compares.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 3, what does Meron's account explain that the storage view could not?
choices: Why a list studied a few minutes earlier is usually recalled almost in full
Why people remember some events in detail and forget others entirely
Why the details that people wrongly add to a memory are usually typical of events of that kind
Why unusual events are often remembered with particular accuracy
explanation: The paragraph says the account explains why errors lean toward the typical. (1) is something the account merely accommodates (the storage view handles it too), and (4) is the criticism raised against Meron in paragraph 4.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 4, how did Meron reply to the criticism that unusual events are often remembered with particular accuracy?
choices: She argued that unusual events are in fact remembered less accurately than they seem to be
She argued that the mind retains above all what departs from the typical, because the typical can always be supplied later
She argued that general knowledge includes knowledge of unusual events as well as of typical ones
She argued that young children, who know little about typical events, remember unusual events best
explanation: Her reply is that the mind keeps chiefly what departs from the typical. (4) is not her reply but the consequence that the critics draw from it, and (1) and (3) do not appear in the passage.

steps.stem: What is the structure of the passage?
choices: A view of memory is presented, evidence supporting it is described, two objections to it are raised, and the view is revised in order to meet them
Two views of memory are presented side by side, and an experiment is described that decides between them

A view of memory is presented; two objections to it are raised; an alternative account is presented along with the evidence that supports it; and an objection to that account, the reply to it and a difficulty that the reply raises are described
A view of memory is presented along with two objections to it; an alternative account is then presented, and the passage concludes that it has overcome all the difficulties of the earlier view
explanation: Paragraph 1 presents the storage view, paragraph 2 the two objections, paragraph 3 Meron's account and its support, and paragraph 4 a criticism, her reply and a new difficulty. (4) ignores the open ending, and (1) wrongly has the storage view revised.

steps.stem: Which assumption is necessary in order to conclude from the findings of the study described in paragraph 1 that diners reward good service with larger tips?
choices: That the servers taking part in the study preferred serving attentively to serving as usual
That the diners knew that the servers had been asked to serve some of the tables with special attentiveness
That the diners seated at the tables served attentively did not differ from the other diners in any other respect that affects the size of a tip
That diners in every city leave the same share of the bill as a tip
explanation: The study attributes the larger tips to the attentive service; this holds only if the two groups of tables differed in nothing else that affects tipping. (2) would, if anything, weaken the conclusion, and (1) and (4) are not needed for it.

steps.stem: From Halevi's words in paragraph 2 it follows that, in her view, the difference between the results of the earlier case and those of the recent study stems from -
choices: the fact that in the earlier case the experienced servers were replaced, whereas in the recent study the staff remained the same
the fact that the recent study was conducted in a country where tipping is not customary
the fact that in the earlier case a service charge was added to the prices, whereas in the recent study no charge was added
the fact that in the recent study the servers regarded the abolition of tipping as unwelcome
explanation: Halevi attributes the fall in ratings to the loss of experienced staff, and the recent study differs precisely in keeping its staff. (3) invents a difference the passage does not state, (2) confuses the study with the remark about Japan, and (4) is a detail that did not affect the ratings.

steps.stem: Suppose the diners' ratings of the service in the two cases described in paragraph 2 were plotted on a graph against the months since tipping was abolished, with a solid line for the earlier case and a dashed line for the recent study. Which of the following descriptions of the graph is consistent with paragraph 2?
choices: Both lines fall steeply from the same starting point
The solid line remains level; the dashed line falls steeply
The solid line falls steeply; the dashed line falls gradually
The solid line falls steeply; the dashed line remains level
explanation: In the earlier case ratings fell steeply; in the recent study they did not fall at all. (3) is the tempting half-right choice, but the passage says the ratings in the recent study did not fall at all, and (2) reverses the lines.

steps.stem: Which of the following explanations could be offered, according to Halevi's approach, for the fact that in a certain city, tips given for meals delivered to the home are much smaller than tips given in restaurants?
choices: The service provided by delivery workers is of lower quality than the service provided by restaurant servers
Tips for delivered meals are usually added in an app when the customer is alone, so no one whose regard the customer wishes to keep sees them
Customers are unlikely to meet the same delivery worker again, so there is no reason to encourage good service in the future
People who order meals to their homes usually earn less than people who eat in restaurants
explanation: For Halevi, a tip is worth what its audience makes of it, and a tip given where no one sees it is worth nothing. (1) is the explanation of the accepted view, and (3) fails because, as paragraph 3 notes, people tip generously even where they will never return.

steps.stem:
According to paragraph 3, how would Halevi rank the following tips according to their value to the person who gives them, from the greatest to the smallest?
I. A tip added in an app while the diner is alone at home
II. A tip left at the table in view of a business partner whom the diner wishes to impress
III. A tip left at the table by a diner eating alone among strangers
choices: III, II, I
II, I, III
I, III, II
II, III, I
explanation: Halevi's quotation sets the order: witnesses whose regard one wishes to keep (II), then strangers (III), then no witnesses at all (I). (1) swaps the first two, and (2) places the unseen tip above the one seen by strangers.

steps.stem: What is the structure of the passage?
choices: A prevailing explanation of a custom is presented along with its supporting evidence; an alternative explanation is proposed, based on a critique of that evidence and on a new reading of an earlier case; the alternative is developed; and a way of testing it is described
Two explanations of a custom are presented, and the results of an experiment are described that decide in favor of the second
An explanation of a custom is presented, criticisms of it are raised, and the passage shows how the explanation can be defended against them
A custom is described, the reasons for its spread across different countries are examined, and it is predicted that it will soon disappear
explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the accepted view and its evidence, paragraph 2 Halevi's critique and reinterpretation, paragraph 3 her positive theory, and paragraph 4 a test whose result is still unknown. (2) wrongly treats the test as decided, and (3) reverses who wins the argument.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 1, which of the following is not correct regarding the cylinders found in the schoolhouse?
choices: The damp of the cellar softened the wax, and many of the cylinders cracked as a result
They were recorded by the village teacher, who asked his neighbors to sing
Some of the recordings on them were lost when they were first played
They preserve songs as the villagers sang them, not as collectors wrote them down
explanation: The paragraph says that heat softens wax, which the cool cellar prevented; the damp caused mold, and the cracks came from the pressure of the crate. (3) is correct: the old stylus scraped away part of the groove.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 2, why did the development of electrical transfer revive the hope of hearing the whole collection?
choices: Because it made it possible to play cylinders that had broken into pieces
Because it removed completely the hiss that covers old recordings
Because it had been developed especially for collections of folk songs
Because it read the groove with a stylus light enough not to wear down the wax
explanation: The old stylus had destroyed grooves; the new method reads them without wearing them down. (1) is exactly what the method could not do (paragraph 3), (2) overstates "reduce" as "remove completely," and (3) confuses the collections it was used on with its origin.

steps.stem: Which of the following claims is not correct regarding the "collections of folk songs" mentioned in paragraph 2?
choices: They were recorded early in the twentieth century
They were recorded by composers who traveled from village to village
They were transferred to a modern medium only after optical scanning had been developed
They were recorded on wax cylinders
explanation: The paragraph cites these collections as having been transferred by electrical transfer, so the claim that they had to wait for optical scanning is false. The other three claims are stated or implied in the same sentence.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 3, why was electrical transfer of no use for most of the cylinders in the crate?
choices: Because the stylus of the modern machine was too heavy for wax that had been weakened by mold
Because the stylus follows the groove as the cylinder turns, and the cracks interrupted the groove while broken cylinders could not be turned at all
Because the earliest recordings in the collection were too faint for the stylus to register
Because the filters applied to the signal could not separate the singing from the hiss
explanation: The paragraph explains that reading depends on riding along a continuous, rotating groove, which cracks and fragments prevent. (1) contradicts the lightness stressed in paragraph 2, and (3) and (4) are not mentioned.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, which of the following sentences correctly describes the difference between electrical transfer and optical scanning?
choices: The first converts the motion of a stylus into sound, whereas the second produces only an image of the surface
The first wears down the wax, whereas the second leaves it untouched
The first reads the groove itself, whereas the second reads the color of the wax around it
Both read the groove, but the first follows it by contact while the cylinder turns, whereas the second measures its shape without contact and without rotation
explanation: Both methods read the groove; they differ in how - contact and rotation versus measurement from above. (1) is wrong because the computer converts the calculated motion into sound, (2) contradicts paragraph 2, and (3) invents a property of the surface.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, what occurred in 2016?
choices: Songs were recovered from several of the broken cylinders by a method that does not touch them
All the songs in the collection were recovered from the cylinders
A method for reading broken cylinders was invented especially for the collection
The broken cylinders were glued together and played on a modern machine
explanation: In 2016 the team recovered the songs on several broken cylinders by optical scanning. (2) overstates the result (only some forty songs so far), (3) ignores that the method came from inspecting machine parts, and (4) describes the approach that failed.

steps.stem: Why is the closure of the city's shipyards mentioned in paragraph 1?
choices: To explain why the number of shops in the market fell after 1950
To show that the decline of the quarter was part of a general decline of the city's economy
To explain why the decline of the quarter received little attention beyond the city
To give an example of the damage that the floods caused in the city
explanation: The closure appears in the sentence explaining why the quarter's fate drew little outside attention. (1) and (2) turn it into a cause of the decline, which the passage attributes to other factors, and (4) confuses it with the floods mentioned beside it.

steps.stem: Which of the following claims is implied by paragraph 3?
choices: The income from the souvenir kiosks around the coach parks goes to the city
Some of the quarter's traders have adapted their products to a clientele that the road brought to the quarter
The bakers of the quarter now earn more than they did before the road was built
Most of the tourists who visit the quarter return to it several times
explanation: The bakers now sell smaller pastries to tourists brought by the coaches. (1) is contradicted - the kiosks belong to companies from the capital, and the city's income comes from parking fees; (3) contradicts "much smaller"; (4) contradicts "customers who will never return."

steps.stem: According to the explanation that was assumed in paragraph 4, what is the order of events that led to the "further danger"?
choices: Vibrations from the traffic - the foundations sank unevenly - the soil settled - the soil loosened - the walls cracked
The groundwater level fell - the piles rotted - the foundations sank unevenly - the walls cracked
The soil loosened - vibrations from the traffic - the soil settled - the walls cracked - the foundations sank unevenly
Vibrations from the traffic - the soil loosened - the soil settled - the foundations sank unevenly - the walls cracked
explanation: The assumed explanation runs: traffic shakes the ground, the soil loosens, settles, the foundations sink and the walls crack. (2) is the engineers' explanation, not the assumed one, and (1) and (3) scramble the chain.

steps.stem: Suppose a new means of transport were introduced in Lendra, and within a few years the condition of the market quarter and of its traders improved considerably. Which of the following is best suited to be that means of transport?
choices: A shuttle bus between the coach parks and the city's airport, for tourists only
A tram line that stops at the market gate and links it with the residential districts on the far side of the ring road
A second, wider ring road farther from the quarter, which would draw the heavy traffic away from it
An underground railway with a station beneath the market, whose tunnels must be kept dry by constant pumping of groundwater
explanation: Such a tram restores what the road took away - shoppers and the walking customers from across the road - without harming the piles. (4) brings customers but lowers the groundwater and speeds the rot; (3) moves traffic away but brings no customers; (1) serves only tourists.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, what did the examination of the wooden piles reveal?
choices: That the rot in the piles had begun before the ring road was built
That the vibrations of the traffic were the only cause of the damage to the houses
That the piles had never been submerged in groundwater
That the pumping by the breweries and dye works began only after the ring road was built
explanation: The engineers found that the rot began before the road, in the years when industry started pumping groundwater. (2) is the assumption the piles contradicted, and (4) reverses the order of events.

steps.stem: Following their studies, Vos and the engineers from the technical university publish a joint article presenting their shared conclusions. Which of the following titles is best suited to it?
choices: "The Ring Road: Sole Cause of the Decline of Lendra's Market Quarter"
"Industry, Not Traffic: What Emptied Lendra's Market"
"How the Ring Road Emptied the Market and Hastened the Decay of the Timber Houses"
"The Ring Road as a Blessing for Lendra's Old Quarter"
explanation: Vos holds that the road drove away the shoppers; the engineers found that it hastened a decay that industry began. (1) ignores the engineers' finding, (2) contradicts Vos, and (4) is the city council's view.

steps.stem: Standard time "does not appear on such lists" (paragraph 1) - that is, it is not usually counted among -
choices: the arrangements on which people rely many times a day
the agreements that were reached only after years of dispute
the great machines through which histories of technology tell the story of the modern world
the innovations that required no discovery
explanation: The "lists" are the great machines named in the previous sentence. (1) is exactly what the paragraph says standard time is, (2) describes it too (paragraph 3), and (4) reverses the point: it involved no discovery.

steps.stem: The sentence "Yet its effect on everyday life has been enormous" (paragraph 1) is given below four times, each time with a different word or words stressed (in capital letters). Which of the stresses best expresses the sentence's intent in the passage?
choices: Yet ITS effect on everyday life has been enormous
Yet its effect on everyday life has been ENORMOUS
Yet its effect on EVERYDAY life has been enormous
Yet its effect on everyday life HAS BEEN enormous
explanation: "Yet" contrasts the size of the effect with the modesty of the means just described (no machine, no discovery). Stressing "its" would imply that the great machines had a smaller effect, "everyday" would contrast with some other area of life the passage never mentions, and "has been" would contrast past with future.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 2, why did the differences between the times kept in different towns cause no harm before the railways?
choices: Because travel was so slow that a traveler hardly noticed a difference of a few minutes between the time of one place and that of another
Because every town set its clocks by the sun, so the time kept in each town was accurate
Because the clocks of towns a hundred kilometers apart showed the same time
Because travelers set their watches by the clocks of the stations they passed
explanation: The paragraph ties the harmlessness to slow travel: someone days on the road did not notice the drift. (2) is true but does not explain why the differences did no harm, (3) contradicts the paragraph (such clocks differed by minutes), and (4) belongs to the railway age.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 3, what would have happened if each country had counted its time zones from a meridian of its own?
choices: Ships would have had to replace the charts by which they navigated
Each country would have had to set its clocks by reference to a place outside its borders
France would have gone on keeping Paris time until 1911
The zones of neighboring countries would not have fit together
explanation: The paragraph states that zones fit those of neighboring countries only if all are measured from a common meridian. (2) is the price of the common meridian, not of separate ones; (1) is what choosing a line other than Greenwich would have caused; (3) is what actually happened, not a consequence of the hypothetical.

steps.stem: According to paragraphs 2 and 3, in which of the following options are the events presented in the correct chronological order?
choices: The railroads of North America adopt time zones - most British railways adopt London time - delegates meet in Washington - France adopts a time based on Greenwich
Most British railways adopt London time - the railroads of North America adopt time zones - delegates meet in Washington - France adopts a time based on Greenwich
Most British railways adopt London time - delegates meet in Washington - the railroads of North America adopt time zones - France adopts a time based on Greenwich
Most British railways adopt London time - the railroads of North America adopt time zones - delegates meet in Washington - most of the world's ships begin to navigate by charts drawn from Greenwich
explanation: 1840s, 1883, 1884, 1911. (1) and (3) each swap two events, and (4) places the use of Greenwich charts after the conference, although the ships "already" used them, which is why Greenwich was chosen.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, on which of the following questions are opinions divided?
choices: Whether the advantages of a uniform time have outweighed its drawbacks
Whether standard time has shaped everyday life
Whether the official clock in western China departs from the position of the sun
Whether the railroads introduced standard time in order to impose their own hour on communities
explanation: "Whether the uniformity has been worth what it cost is a matter of opinion." (2) is what the passage says is not a matter of opinion, (3) is presented as a fact, and (4) is the view of the nineteenth-century protesters, not a question the passage presents as open.

steps.stem: Noa and Amir heard Tirosh's conclusion and argued that their own preferences could serve as evidence in its favor. Which of the following best describes Noa's and Amir's preferences?
choices: Noa and Amir both find the name "Rex" too harsh for their new puppy, and both prefer the name "Lulabel"
Noa wants to call their new puppy "Rex," a name that Amir finds harsh, and Amir wants to call it "Lulabel," a name that Noa finds silly
Noa and Amir both like the name "Rex" for their new puppy, although Noa likes it more than Amir does
Noa preferred the name "Rex" for their new puppy at first, but after hearing Amir's reasons she came to prefer "Lulabel," as he does
explanation: Tirosh found that a name one group likes is rejected by the others, so no name pleases everyone; only (2) shows each person's favorite rejected by the other. (1) and (3) show agreement, and (4) shows preferences converging, which is evidence against the conclusion.

steps.stem: Which of the following arises from paragraph 2 regarding the "O.K. Clubs" formed in 1840?
choices: They coined the abbreviation "O.K." as a campaign slogan
They helped Van Buren win the election of 1840
They opposed the writers of usage guides who regarded the word as vulgar
Without them, "O.K." would probably have been forgotten like most of the other abbreviations
explanation: The paragraph says most of the jokes were soon forgotten and that "O.K." was "saved by an accident of politics," the clubs. (1) ignores that the abbreviation existed in Boston in the 1830s, (2) contradicts "Van Buren lost," and (3) links two things the paragraph never connects.

steps.stem:
According to the passage, which of the following completes the sentence below correctly?
"The fact that "OK" ____ could strengthen ____."
choices: can be written with two capital letters that are familiar far beyond the countries that use the Latin alphabet / the explanation presented in paragraph 4
was first used in newspapers in Boston / the explanation presented in paragraph 3
is used more often by immigrants in their first months in a new country than by those who have lived there for years / the explanation presented in paragraph 4
contains sounds that are missing from several widely spoken languages / the explanation presented in paragraph 3
explanation: Newcomers are the speakers most afraid of sounding foreign, so their heavier use of a word that sounds foreign to no one supports the explanation from reluctance (paragraph 4). (1) is one of the five features listed in paragraph 3, so it bears on that explanation, not on paragraph 4; (2) is irrelevant to either explanation; (4) would weaken paragraph 3, which relies on sounds found in nearly every language.

steps.stem: According to paragraph 2, which of the following characteristics is not common to "O.W." and "O.K.", but belongs to only one of them?
choices: It spread across the country as a political slogan
It abbreviated a deliberately misspelled phrase
It appeared in Boston newspapers in the late 1830s
It was meant to amuse newspaper readers
explanation: Only "O.K." was taken up by the Van Buren campaign. The other three describe the whole family of Boston abbreviations, "O.W." included.

steps.stem: Which of the following claims is implied by the last paragraph?
choices: Immigrant children who use "OK" learn the language of their new country faster than those who do not
People today no longer feel reluctant to use words that mark them as outsiders
Travelers use "OK" mainly because it is the only word they know in the language of the country they visit
People who share no language may prefer to remain silent rather than use words that could make them sound foreign
explanation: The paragraph says the reluctance obstructs conversation because each side hesitates to speak for fear of sounding foreign, which implies (4). (1) turns joining conversation into learning the language faster, (2) contradicts "a reluctance they cannot simply decide to abandon," and (3) gives a reason the paragraph does not give.

steps.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the claims made in the passage?
choices: A linguist searched for a word that would please speakers of every language and found one, "OK," whose success is explained by its sounds and by the needs of travelers
"OK" is an exception to the conclusion that no word pleases everyone; it spread because newspaper writers in Boston promoted it more than their other abbreviations
A study concluded that no word appeals to speakers of every language; "OK" is an exception whose history is traced, and two explanations of its wide acceptance are presented
Speakers of different languages prefer different sounds, so a company that sells its products worldwide should choose a different name for each region, as the history of "OK" shows
explanation: The passage moves from Tirosh's conclusion, to the exception and its history, to two explanations. (1) contradicts her finding, (2) invents the cause of the spread (it was politics), and (4) draws a business recommendation that the passage never makes and misuses the history of "OK."

steps.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the findings of Halm's study described in paragraph 1?
choices: The Egyptian paintings depict their scenes in great detail but give almost no indication of how near or far things are, and they show some objects in ways that seem strange to us
The Egyptian painters saw depth less clearly than we do, because the human eye had not yet completed its development
The Egyptian paintings show important figures larger than others because such figures stand nearer to the viewer
The Egyptian paintings depict gardens and banquets from above, as they would appear to a person looking down from a height
explanation: The findings are what Halm observed: detailed scenes, almost no depth, and oddities such as the pool and the trees. (2) is his interpretation, not his finding; (3) contradicts "wherever they happen to stand"; (4) generalizes the single example of the pool.

steps.stem: Why is it noted in paragraph 2 that Darwin's theory "had been published less than a decade earlier"?
choices: To show that Halm based his claim on observations that Darwin had made
To explain how Wendt was able to extend Halm's claim
To explain why Halm's claim seemed bold at the time it was made
To suggest that Halm's claim was mistaken because it relied on a new theory
explanation: The sentence opens with "Halm's claim was a bold one" and gives the youth of the theory as the reason. (1) and (2) invent links, and (4) passes a judgment the paragraph does not make; the physiological claim is rejected later, and for other reasons.

steps.stem: Which of the following descriptions fits both Halm's study and Wendt's study?
choices: It examined the earliest surviving pictures of many cultures
It identified a fixed order in which the devices for showing depth appeared
It compared the way depth is shown in pictures with the way living people judge distances
It explained a feature of old pictures by the state of development of the eye of the people who made them
explanation: Both men attributed what they saw in pictures to the development of the eye. (1) and (2) describe Wendt's study only (Halm studied Egypt alone), and (3) describes the twentieth-century research in paragraph 3.

steps.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the findings described in paragraph 3 regarding peoples whose traditions of picture-making made no use of perspective?
choices: They judged depth in drawings correctly, but misjudged real distances
They often misread depth in drawings, but judged real distances as accurately as anyone else
They could not tell which of two figures in a drawing was drawn larger
They saw depth less clearly than people whose traditions use perspective
explanation: Participants misread the hunting drawing yet judged real distances accurately: convention limits depiction, not seeing. (1) reverses the two findings, (3) invents a difficulty, and (4) is Halm's view, which the research refuted.

steps.stem: Why is a sketch of the way to a person's house mentioned in paragraph 4?
choices: To illustrate a picture that shows how things are arranged rather than how they look from a single spot
To show that the Egyptian painters drew maps rather than pictures
To give an example of a picture that uses a single vanishing point
To show that people who cannot see depth clearly draw maps instead of views
explanation: The sketch is a familiar case of drawing what things are and where they are, as Schäfer says the Egyptian painter did. (2) takes the comparison literally, (3) is the opposite of the point, and (4) brings back the physiological explanation the passage rejects.

steps.stem: Which of the following claims is correct according to the explanation offered in paragraph 4 for the fixed order in which the devices for showing depth appeared?
choices: Linear perspective appeared last because it is the hardest device for the eye to perceive
Every tradition of picture-making eventually adopted a single vanishing point
Overlapping appeared first because it was invented in Egypt and spread from there
A device appeared early in a tradition if pictures in that tradition could hardly do without it
explanation: The explanation is need: overlapping is needed in almost any scene, a vanishing point only when a picture is meant as a window. (1) is a physiological reason, which the passage abandons; (2) contradicts "only in some cultures"; (3) invents a history of diffusion.

steps.stem: In paragraph 3, the saying "Time is money" is presented as -
choices: a claim about the value of time that the author of the passage wishes to refute
a sentence that the procedure described in the paragraph renders ungrammatical
an example of a rule that the reader must reconstruct from the text alone
a familiar saying whose strangeness is concealed by its usual wording
explanation: The definitions procedure lets the reader "suddenly notice how strange a claim it makes," a strangeness the familiar wording had concealed. (1) turns an illustration into an argument, (2) invents an effect: the rewritten sentence is perfectly grammatical, and (3) belongs to the last sentence of the paragraph.

steps.stem: "The reader must reconstruct it from the text alone" (paragraph 3) - that is, in such works the rule plays a larger part than in -
choices: works in which the procedure is known to the reader, like those described earlier in the paragraph
works written without any rule at all
the messages from which a cryptographer reconstructs a code
works that exclude a letter, like "La Disparition"
explanation: "A still larger part" compares these works with the procedures just described, whose rules are known. (2) is not discussed, (3) takes the comparison with the cryptographer literally, and (4) picks a work from another paragraph that the comparison does not concern.

steps.stem: The description of "Easter Wings" (paragraph 4) is presented as an illustration of -
choices: a work whose rule the reader must reconstruct from the text alone
a work in which the arrangement of the lines on the page contributes to what the work says
a work that deliberately excludes something that ordinary writing takes for granted
a work whose shape serves mainly as a decoration of its text
explanation: The paragraph presents the visual feature and insists that the shape "is one of the things that the words say." (1) and (3) belong to paragraphs 3 and 2, and (4) contradicts "The shape is not an ornament."

steps.stem: The question raised at the beginning of paragraph 6 follows from the fact that -
choices: constrained writing uses familiar signs such as letters and words
some constrained works are addressed to readers of literature
readers who come to constrained works from puzzles tend to enjoy them more than practiced readers of literature
"La Disparition" runs to some three hundred pages without the letter e
explanation: "Then" refers back to paragraph 5: if puzzle lovers enjoy these works more than readers of literature, one may ask whether they belong to the world of puzzles. (2) is part of the answer, not its ground; (1) is true but does not raise the question; (4) is an unrelated detail.

steps.stem: According to the last paragraph, why do certain constrained works require a reader who notices the rule?
choices: Because in these works the rule is never announced
Because only such a reader can see that the form expresses something that the words alone do not
Because the pleasure these works offer lies chiefly in finding the rule
Because these works are addressed mainly to lovers of puzzles
explanation: The paragraph gives the reason explicitly: "only such a reader can see that the form is saying something the words alone do not." (1) comes from paragraph 3, (3) describes the other kind of work (palindromes), and (4) reverses "addressed to readers of literature."

steps.stem: What answer does the passage give to the question raised in the last paragraph?
choices: Constrained writing belongs to literature, since every constrained work obeys rules of its own
Constrained writing belongs to the world of puzzles, since the pleasure it offers lies in solving
Some constrained works are chiefly puzzles, while others, in which the rule creates the meaning, belong to literature
The question cannot be answered, since the answer depends on what each reader expects
explanation: "The answer is not clear-cut": palindromes are mainly puzzles, while works like Perec's and Herbert's are addressed to readers of literature. (1) and (2) each take one side for all works, and (4) borrows "expectation" from paragraph 5 and turns a divided answer into no answer.

vop-01.title: Passage 1
paragraphs: Biologists have long observed that island animals often differ in size from their closest relatives on the mainland, and in a predictable direction: species that are large on the mainland tend to become smaller on islands, while species that are small tend to become larger. The fossil record offers striking cases of the first kind. Several Mediterranean islands, Sicily and Malta among them, were once home to dwarf elephants, some of which stood barely a meter high at the shoulder. A living case of the second kind is a rat on the Indonesian island of Flores that weighs several times as much as the common rat. The pattern, however, is a tendency rather than a law: a great many island species do not differ in size from their mainland relatives at all, and a few have changed in the direction opposite to the one that the pattern predicts.

The most widely accepted explanation concerns food. An island offers a limited supply of food, and its animals cannot move elsewhere when that supply runs short. A large body requires a great deal of food, whereas a smaller individual of the same species can get through a lean season on what remains. Over many generations, therefore, smaller individuals are more likely to survive and leave offspring, and the population as a whole becomes smaller. Some researchers have proposed a refinement of this explanation, which we will call here the "ration hypothesis." It holds that what matters is not the area of the island but the amount of food it provides for each animal: a large island consisting mostly of bare rock may favor small bodies more strongly than a small island covered with dense vegetation.

A second explanation looks not to food but to enemies. Remote islands often have few large predators or none, since such predators need extensive hunting grounds and seldom cross the sea. On the mainland, being small helps an animal to escape by hiding in cracks and burrows, while being very large protects a grazing animal, since few predators can overcome it. Where there are no predators, both advantages lose their value, and body size is free to shift toward whatever suits local conditions best. The merit of this explanation is that it accounts for both directions of change by a single cause, whereas the explanation from food is more convincing for the shrinking of large animals than for the growth of small ones. Its weakness is that it predicts a change in size on every island that lacks predators, although many such islands are home to species whose size has not changed.

A team of biologists compared the two explanations on a chain of small islands inhabited by a single species of lizard. A predatory snake lives on some of the islands but not on others, and the islands also differ in their vegetation, and hence in the number of insects on which the lizards feed. The researchers reasoned that if the explanation from predators were correct, the lizards on the snake-free islands should differ in size from those on the other islands even where the supply of insects was similar. In fact, the lizards' size corresponded closely to the supply of insects, whereas the presence of snakes made almost no difference. The researchers concluded that on these islands, at least, food is the decisive factor. They added a caution, however: since the snakes reached the islands relatively recently, the lizards may not yet have had time to respond to them.

Neither explanation, then, turns the island pattern into a law. What the island cases do show is something more general: the size of an animal, which we tend to regard as a fixed feature of its species, is in fact a compromise among competing pressures, such as the need for food, the danger from predators and the demands of the climate. When life on an island shifts the balance among these pressures, size shifts with it, and the fossil record suggests that on some islands this happened within a few thousand years, a moment by the standards of evolution.

vop-02.title: Passage 2
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, many psychologists assumed that remembering an event is much like taking a document out of a filing cabinet. According to this "storage" view, every experience leaves in the mind a trace that preserves it exactly as it occurred, so that a given memory is either found intact or not found at all. Forgetting, on this view, is a failure of search, never an alteration of what was stored. The favorite illustration of the storage view was the memorized list: a person who has studied a list of twenty words either recalls a particular word or fails to recall it, and whatever is recalled can be checked against the list. The proponents of the view held that memory for the events of daily life works in exactly the same way, and that research had only to discover the conditions under which traces are stored and found reliably.

This view came under sustained attack. First, its critics argued, a memory does not remain fixed from one occasion of remembering to the next. A person who tells the story of a childhood holiday many times over the years tells a slightly different story each time: a detail is dropped, another is added. Can one say at which telling the story stopped being the original memory - the fifth, say, but not the fourth? The critics held that no such point can be found, since the changes accumulate by steps too small to notice. Second, they argued, the errors of memory are not only omissions. People also remember, with complete confidence, things that never occurred. In a well-known experiment of the 1970s, participants who had watched a short film of a collision between two cars were questioned about it a week later, and a considerable number of them reported having seen broken glass at the scene, although the film showed none. A witness who describes shattered glass at an accident in which no glass was broken has not failed to find a record; they have found a record that was never made.

The psychologist Dalia Meron proposed a different account of remembering. In her view, to remember is not to retrieve a record but to reconstruct an event. What the mind retains is a collection of fragments - an image, a phrase, a feeling - and each time we remember, we rebuild the event from these fragments, filling the gaps with our general knowledge of how events of that kind usually unfold. Meron's account explains what the storage view could not: why the errors of memory are not scattered at random but lean consistently toward the typical, so that what people add to a memory is almost always something that usually happens in such situations. It also accommodates the memorized list, the storage view's favorite illustration: a list studied a few minutes earlier leaves fragments so complete that rebuilding it requires almost no filling at all. In one of Meron's experiments, participants who had read a short story about a visit to a doctor were asked, two weeks later, to retell it. Many of them included details that the story did not contain but that belong to most such visits, such as sitting in a waiting room or being weighed; hardly any included details that do not belong to such visits.

Meron's account has not escaped criticism. Its critics point out that unusual events - precisely the ones that general knowledge cannot supply - are often remembered with particular accuracy, whereas the account would lead one to expect them to be remembered worst of all. Meron replied that the mind does not retain fragments at random: what it retains above all is whatever departs from the typical, since the typical can always be supplied later and the unusual cannot. This reply, however, raises a further difficulty. If the mind retains what departs from the typical, it must already know, at the moment of the experience, what is typical. Young children, who know far less than adults about how events usually unfold, should then retain more of what they experience and remember it more faithfully - whereas the evidence, as far as it goes, suggests that their memories are, if anything, less accurate.

vop-03.title: Passage 3
paragraphs: Tipping has long puzzled economists. In many countries, restaurant diners hand over a sum that they are not legally obliged to pay, often to a server they will never see again, and the custom has proved remarkably durable. The accepted explanation has been that the tip is a payment for quality: diners reward good service and withhold the reward from poor service, and servers, knowing this, have an incentive to serve well. The explanation rests on a large body of findings. In one study, the servers at a group of restaurants were asked to serve half of their tables with special attentiveness - checking on the diners frequently and remembering orders without writing them down - and to serve the other half as usual. The tables that received the attentive service left larger tips. Dozens of similar studies, conducted in different cities and with different measures of quality, have found that a diner's rating of the service predicts the size of the tip, and the finding has been regarded as one of the most secure in the study of consumer behavior.

Recently the economist Tamar Halevi proposed a different explanation. The effect of service on tips, as documented in these studies, is small: a diner who rates the service as excellent tips only a few percentage points more than one who rates it as poor - too little, in her view, for reward to be the main purpose of so widespread a custom. She argues, moreover, that tipping is not necessary for good service at all: if it were, service would be poor wherever tipping is not customary, whereas in Japan, where tipping is not customary, restaurant service is widely regarded as exceptionally attentive. She also reinterprets an earlier case in which a restaurant chain abolished tipping, added a fixed service charge to its prices, and at the same time replaced most of its experienced servers with newly hired ones; in the following months, diners' ratings of the service fell steeply. The cause, Halevi argues, was not the loss of the tip but the loss of the experienced staff. A recent study supports her reading: in another chain, which abolished tipping but kept its entire staff - a change the servers described as unwelcome at first but soon routine - diners' ratings of the service did not fall at all, and remained indistinguishable from those of branches that continued to accept tips.

To understand tipping, Halevi maintains, one must look not at the server but at the audience - at who sees the tip being given. This approach, she claims, accounts for the considerable variation in tipping between people and between situations. Why, for example, do people tip in restaurants they will never visit again, where good service can no longer be encouraged by the promise of a return visit? And why, in her own data, did diners who paid at the table in view of their companions leave larger tips than diners at the same restaurants who paid alone at the counter? Because, according to Halevi, a tip is a signal: it tells those who witness it that the person tipping is generous and can afford to be, and it thereby raises that person's standing in their eyes. "The value of a tip lies in the eyes that see it," she writes. "It is greatest when the witnesses are people whose regard one wishes to keep, smaller when they are strangers, and nothing at all when no one sees it." Halevi regards both observations as evidence that the size of a tip is adjusted to its audience rather than to the quality of the meal.

Halevi's theory is now being tested with a new source of data: the electronic payment terminals used in many restaurants, which record every tip together with the time, the number of diners at the table, and whether the bill was paid at the table or at the counter. If the theory is correct, the tips paid where no one can see them should prove to be the smallest of all. Whether they are, the records will show.

vop-04.title: Passage 4
paragraphs: In 1971, workers renovating an old schoolhouse in a village in the mountains of central Europe found in its cellar a wooden crate holding some two hundred wax cylinders - the medium on which sound was most commonly recorded at the beginning of the twentieth century. The cylinders had been recorded around 1908 by the village teacher, who had carried a phonograph from house to house and asked his neighbors to sing for it. A find of this size is rare. Wax softens in heat and cracks in cold, and the cellar, which stayed cool and dark throughout the year, had spared the cylinders the summers that ruined so many recordings of the period. The shelter, however, had exacted its own price. The damp of the cellar had covered the wax with mold, and the slow swelling and shrinking of the wooden crate had pressed on the cylinders until many of them cracked along their length; some had broken into several pieces. When the first intact cylinders were played on a phonograph of the period, moreover, its heavy stylus scraped away part of the groove, and whatever had been recorded in those turns was lost for good. The cylinders are among the very few records of the region's songs as the villagers themselves sang them, rather than as collectors wrote them down in musical notation, and this explains the effort that has been invested in them.

The development of electrical transfer revived the hope of hearing the whole collection. In this method the cylinder is turned on a modern machine at a precisely controlled speed, and a stylus far lighter than the old ones follows the groove. The stylus moves up and down with the pattern cut into the groove, and its motion is converted into an electrical signal that can be recorded on tape or stored in a computer. Because the stylus presses on the wax so lightly, a cylinder can be played in this way many times without being worn down, and filters applied to the signal reduce the hiss that covers old recordings. Over the past decades archives have transferred many thousands of cylinders by this method, among them collections of folk songs recorded early in the century by composers who traveled from village to village to collect them, and scholars expected it to do the same for the crate from the schoolhouse.

A stylus, however light, can read a groove only by riding along it as the cylinder turns. Along a crack the groove is interrupted, and at each crack the stylus jumped, or caught on the broken edge and chipped it. A cylinder in pieces could not be mounted on the machine or turned at all. For the cracked and broken cylinders, which made up most of the collection, the method that had served other archives so well was of no use, and after a series of trials in the 1980s that left two cylinders more damaged than before, the attempt was abandoned. For thirty years the cylinders stayed on the shelves of a national archive, cleaned, cataloged and silent.

Then, in 2016, a team of physicists and sound engineers recovered the songs on several of the broken cylinders by means of optical scanning. Like electrical transfer, optical scanning reads the groove, but it does not touch it. A microscope passes over the surface of the wax and measures the depth of the groove at millions of points, and a computer assembles the measurements into a three-dimensional map of the surface. From this map the computer calculates the motion that a stylus would have made had it ridden along the groove, and converts that motion into sound. The team's microscope had originally been built for inspecting the surfaces of precision machine parts. Since the method requires neither contact nor rotation, the fragments of a broken cylinder can be scanned one at a time and fitted together on the screen, so that a crack becomes a gap of a fraction of a second in the recording rather than an obstacle to it. Scanning a single cylinder takes about a day, and the team has so far recovered some forty songs.

vop-05.title: Passage 5
paragraphs: The old market quarter of Lendra, a river city in northern Europe, contains one of the largest groups of timber-framed merchants' houses that survive anywhere on the continent, and for five centuries its market was the commercial center of the surrounding province. The quarter is nevertheless in serious decline, and its condition has been worsening steadily since the 1960s. Because of the floods that struck the city in those years, and the closure of its shipyards, which left thousands of workers unemployed, the fate of the quarter drew little attention beyond the city itself. Only in the last decade have heritage organizations begun to survey the quarter systematically and to try to save what remains of its trade. Their first surveys show that of the three hundred shops recorded in the market in 1950, fewer than a hundred are still open.

The urban historian Karin Vos maintains that the principal cause of the decline is the ring road. The road was built around the old quarter in the 1960s by the city's planners, who wished to give the growing number of motorists a fast route in place of the narrow streets through the market, and to replace the trams that had carried shoppers into the quarter since the beginning of the century. The road carries tens of thousands of vehicles a day, but it passes around the quarter without entering it, and the trams, which had stopped at the market gate, were withdrawn. Within twenty years the stream of shoppers had shrunk to a trickle. Moreover, since the road cut the quarter off from the residential districts on its far side, which could now be reached on foot only through a few narrow underpasses, the shopkeepers lost the customers who had once walked in every day. Those who stayed in business were forced to sell at weekly markets in the suburbs, where they paid high fees for their stalls and competed with the supermarkets.

Unlike the shopkeepers, the city council regards the ring road as an unqualified success. The road has brought to the edge of the quarter the coaches of tourists who come to see the timber houses, and the parking fees provide the city with an income it never had before, and a considerable share of its budget for maintaining the streets. The coach parks, like the souvenir kiosks around them, are operated by companies from the capital. The coach parks have changed the lives of the quarter's traders in ways that no one planned. The bakers, for example, who once sold bread to the households of the quarter, now sell small pastries to the tourists waiting beside the coaches - the same dough, shaped smaller and sold at a higher price, to customers who will never return. The trade is much smaller than it was, and far less secure; but it survives, and it remains in the hands of the same families.

A further danger to the quarter is structural: the timber houses have begun to lean, and their walls to crack. This too, it was assumed, was the road's doing. The heavy traffic shook the ground; the vibrations loosened the soil beneath the houses; the loosened soil settled; and as it settled, the foundations sank unevenly and the walls cracked. The explanation went unchallenged for years and was repeated in every report on the quarter. But when engineers from the city's technical university examined the wooden piles on which the houses stand, the piles contradicted it. Wooden piles can last for centuries as long as they remain submerged in groundwater, which keeps from them the oxygen that wood-decaying fungi need; once the water level falls and the wood is exposed to air, they rot. The rot in the piles of the quarter had begun well before the road was built - in precisely the years in which breweries and dye works along the river began to pump large quantities of groundwater for their processes, lowering the water level beneath the quarter. The road, it appears, has hastened a decay that industry began.

vop-06.title: Passage 6
paragraphs: Histories of technology tend to tell the story of the modern world through its great machines: the steam engine, the telegraph, the airplane. Standard time does not appear on such lists. It is not a machine at all, and it involved no discovery; it is simply an agreement that everyone in a given region will set their clocks to the same hour, and that neighboring regions will differ from one another by whole hours. Yet its effect on everyday life has been enormous. A person who wakes to an alarm, catches a train and then joins a call with colleagues on another continent relies on it three times before lunch without giving it a thought.

For most of history every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment at which the sun stood highest, and since the sun reaches that point later the farther west one goes, the clocks of two cities a hundred kilometers apart might differ by several minutes. As long as people traveled on foot or by carriage, the differences did no harm, since a traveler who spent days on the road hardly noticed that their watch no longer agreed with the clocks of their destination. The railways changed this. A train that covered a hundred kilometers in two hours had to run to a timetable, and a timetable is meaningless unless everyone who reads it agrees on what the time is. Each railroad therefore ran on the time of its own headquarters, and a large station might display several clocks, one for each company, all showing different hours. The British railways were the first to respond: during the 1840s most of them adopted London time along their entire networks. In North America, where the distances were far greater, a single time was impractical, and on November 18, 1883, the railroads of the United States and Canada replaced the dozens of times they had been using with a few broad zones, each an hour apart from the next.

The decisive step, however, was not the zones themselves but agreement on the line from which they were counted. For the zones of one country to fit those of its neighbors, all of them had to be measured from a common meridian, and every country had to accept that its clocks would be set by reference to a place outside its own borders. Agreement took years. In 1884 delegates of twenty-five countries met in Washington and chose the meridian that passes through the observatory at Greenwich, near London. The choice was not a scientific one, since any meridian would have served; it was made because the great majority of the world's ships already navigated by charts drawn from Greenwich, and the adoption of any other line would have obliged their owners to replace those charts. The countries that had been counting from meridians of their own were the losers. France, which had measured longitude from Paris for two centuries, abstained in the vote and kept Paris time until 1911, when it adopted a time based on Greenwich but defined it in law, without naming Greenwich, as Paris time set back by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds. The debate was conducted by astronomers and diplomats, but its outcome was determined chiefly by the commercial weight of those who had already committed themselves.

Like most conventions, standard time has not served everyone equally. A zone is a compromise, and the farther a town lies from the center of its zone, the further its clocks depart from its sun. China, which has kept a single time zone since 1949 although the country spans roughly five geographical ones, is the extreme case: in its far west the sun reaches its highest point at around three in the afternoon by the official clock, and many residents keep an unofficial local time alongside the national one. In the nineteenth century, too, newspapers and preachers in some American towns protested against what they called "railroad time," a company's hour imposed on communities that had always taken their hour from the sky. Whether the uniformity has been worth what it cost is a matter of opinion. That it governs our days is not.

vop-07.title: Passage 7
paragraphs: When the cosmetics company Varela hired the linguist Dafna Tirosh in 1996 to find a brand name that would sound appealing in every market, it expected her to produce a single winning word. Tirosh invented some two hundred words, had them read aloud to speakers of fourteen languages and asked the listeners to rate how pleasant each one sounded. The results dismayed the company: there was no word that a majority of the listeners rated highly. The listeners fell instead into three groups: those who preferred short words with hard consonants, such as "Tak"; those who preferred long words made of soft sounds, such as "Lomela"; and those who preferred words that resembled a word in their own language. A name that one group liked was rated poorly by the other two. There is no word that pleases everyone, Tirosh concluded, and the search for one had been mistaken from the start. The company ordered a second survey before it accepted her conclusion.

Tirosh's conclusion has since been confirmed for names of many kinds, but one word is a striking exception: "OK." Speakers of dozens of languages use it in everyday conversation, and it is often described as the most widely understood word in the world. Its story begins in Boston in the late 1830s, when newspaper writers amused their readers with abbreviations of deliberately misspelled phrases: "O.W." for "oll wright," "K.Y." for "know yuse" and "O.K." for "oll korrect." Most of these jokes were forgotten within a season or two. "O.K." was saved by an accident of politics. In 1840 supporters of President Martin Van Buren, who was nicknamed "Old Kinderhook" after the town in New York where he was born, formed "O.K. Clubs," and the letters spread across the country as a campaign slogan. Van Buren lost the election, but the word outlived the campaign and passed from political slang into ordinary speech. For decades afterward, writers of usage guides urged their readers to avoid it as vulgar; the readers took no notice.

Why has "OK" succeeded where other words fail? One explanation, proposed by phoneticians, is that it combines, in balance, five features that make a word easy to borrow. Its sounds, or close substitutes for them, exist in nearly every language, so no speaker has to learn a new sound in order to say it. It is short enough to say in a single breath, yet its two syllables make it hard to mishear. It can be written with two capital letters that are familiar far beyond the countries that use the Latin alphabet. Its form never changes, whatever the sentence around it. And its tone is neither formal nor rude. Most words have two or three of these features. "Affirmative" cannot be misheard, but it is long and stiff; "yeah" is short and friendly, but it is easily lost in noise. "OK" has all five, and none of them at the expense of another. The explanation also accounts for the fate of the words that were offered as replacements for it over the years: each of them gained one advantage by giving up another.

Another explanation appeals to the reluctance of people to use words that mark them as outsiders. This reluctance presumably served people well in the past, when a stranger's unfamiliar speech could be a sign that they were not to be trusted; today it mainly obstructs conversation between people who share no language, each of whom hesitates to speak for fear of sounding foreign. Travelers, however, have found a practical use for "OK." Because it has been adopted by speakers of so many languages, it no longer sounds foreign to anyone, and a tourist and a shopkeeper who have not a single other word in common can close a sale with it. In one survey, teachers of immigrant children reported that newcomers who used "OK" from their first day joined classroom conversation within weeks, while those who did not often remained silent for months. "OK," in other words, is not merely a word but a means by which speakers get around a reluctance that they cannot simply decide to abandon.

vop-08.title: Passage 8
paragraphs: In 1868 the German art historian Ludwig Halm published a study of the wall paintings in the tombs of ancient Egypt, some of which are more than four thousand years old. His most surprising finding concerned depth. The paintings depict gardens, banquets and processions in minute detail, yet they show almost nothing of how near or far things are. A figure in the foreground is no larger than a figure behind it, and a nobleman is drawn taller than his servants wherever they happen to stand. Stranger still, a rectangular garden pool is shown as if seen from above, while the trees that surround it lie flat on the ground, pointing outward in every direction. Halm argued that these pictures were made by people who saw depth less clearly than we do. The reason, in his view, was that the human eye had not yet completed its development.

Halm's claim was a bold one: Darwin's theory of evolution had been published less than a decade earlier, and the idea that a human sense could change within recorded history seemed far-fetched even to many of the theory's supporters. Nevertheless, the claim was taken up. A few years later the art historian Erich Wendt examined the earliest surviving pictures of many cultures and found that the devices for showing depth had appeared in a fixed order. The first was overlapping, in which one figure is partly hidden behind another. Next came placement, in which distant figures are drawn higher up in the picture. Then came diminution, in which distant things are drawn smaller. The last to appear, and only in some cultures, was a single vanishing point toward which all parallel lines converge. Wendt held that this order recorded a gradual change in the eye itself, and in this he went well beyond Halm, who had spoken of a single stage. The physiological part of Wendt's claim was soon abandoned, but the order he described outlived it and shaped much of the later work on the subject.

In the twentieth century researchers set out to test whether the source of the phenomenon really lay in the eye. They worked with peoples whose own traditions of picture-making made no use of perspective. The first results seemed to support Halm and Wendt. Shown a drawing of a hunter, an antelope near him and an elephant drawn small on a distant hill, many participants said that the hunter was aiming at the elephant, which stood closer to his spear on the page. Yet the same people judged distances in their own surroundings as accurately as anyone else, as their skill in hunting and herding required. Their eyes, evidently, registered what their pictures did not show. Studies in other regions reached the same result: the conventions of a culture limit how depth is depicted, not how it is seen.

Why, then, did the Egyptians draw the pool from above and the trees lying flat? The Egyptologist Heinrich Schäfer proposed that the Egyptian painter set out to show what each thing is rather than how it looks from one spot. A pool is a rectangle, so it was drawn as a rectangle; a tree stands upright at the pool's edge, so it was drawn upright, rising from the edge. Something similar happens when a person is asked to sketch the way to their house: they draw a map, not the view from a street corner. But if the eye is not the issue, why the fixed order? One answer is that overlapping is needed as soon as one figure stands in front of another, which happens in almost every scene with more than one figure, so every tradition needed it early. A single vanishing point, by contrast, becomes necessary only when a picture is meant to be seen as if through a window, from one fixed position, and few traditions asked this of their pictures. When painters and architects in fifteenth-century Florence began to ask it, the rules of linear perspective were set down within a few decades.

vop-09.title: Passage 9
paragraphs: In everyday usage, a "constraint" is a limitation: something that prevents a person from doing what they would otherwise do. Writers of the literary genre known as constrained writing use the word in a different sense. For them a constraint is not an obstacle placed in the way of a work but the rule from which the work grows, and a text written under a constraint is not a weaker version of a free one. Such texts obey rules of their own, and a reader who does not notice the rule will find much of what they read arbitrary or clumsy.

The best-known feature of constrained writing is the deliberate exclusion of something that ordinary writing takes for granted. The most celebrated example is the French novel "La Disparition," published by Georges Perec in 1969, which runs to some three hundred pages without once using the letter e, the most common letter in French. What might seem a mere feat of endurance is in fact the subject of the book: its plot concerns a series of disappearances, and its characters sense that something is missing from their world without ever being able to name it. The constraint, in other words, is not a trick played on the reader alongside the story; it is the story, told a second time in the alphabet itself.

A second feature is the use of mechanical procedures that give familiar words unfamiliar meanings. In one such procedure, each word of a sentence is replaced by its dictionary definition. Applied to the saying "Time is money," it produces something like "The continued progress of existence is a medium of exchange," and a reader who meets the saying in this form suddenly notices how strange a claim it makes, a strangeness that its familiar wording had concealed. In some constrained works the rule plays a still larger part: it is never announced, and the reader must reconstruct it from the text alone, much as a cryptographer reconstructs a code from the messages written in it.

Some constrained works have a visual feature as well: their lines are arranged on the page so as to form a shape. In "Easter Wings," published by the English poet George Herbert in 1633, each of the two stanzas is printed so that its lines narrow and then widen again, forming a pair of wings. The shape is not an ornament. The lines grow shortest precisely where the poem speaks of human decline, at the words "Most poore" and "Most thinne," and lengthen again as it speaks of rising. The reader must decide whether they are reading a poem or looking at a picture, and the poem allows no single answer, since the picture is one of the things that the words say.

Constrained writing, then, uses familiar signs - letters, words, the printed line - but combines them under rules that the reader does not expect. Practiced readers of literature often find such works harder than readers who come to them from word games and puzzles. The practiced reader treats every choice in a text as the expression of a meaning, and looks for it even where a word was chosen only because it lacks a certain letter; when the search fails, they are frustrated. The puzzle lover, who expects a rule rather than a message, looks for the rule, finds it and is delighted. The difference lies not in ability but in expectation.

It may be asked, then, whether constrained writing belongs to literature at all, or rather to the world of puzzles. The answer is not clear-cut. There are constrained works, such as collections of palindromes (sentences that read the same backward and forward, like "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"), whose pleasure lies chiefly in the solving, and which have little more to offer once the rule has been found. But there are others in which the rule is the source of the meaning, as in Perec's novel or Herbert's poem, and these require a reader who notices the rule, since only such a reader can see that the form is saying something the words alone do not. Works of this kind, although they are built like puzzles, are addressed to readers of literature.
